title: The church in the south
hookLine: the typical Christian today is a young African or Latin American woman

cards: Early Sunday in a West African city. A young woman irons a dress by lamplight, wakes her little brother, and walks him across town to a church that meets in a school classroom. She leads the choir.
She teaches the children's class. On Wednesday she'll sit with a sick neighbor and pray with her. She holds no title.
And yet some historians of world Christianity say that if you want one face for the church today, hers is a good candidate: young, female, African or Latin American.

teach.h: THE CENTER OF GRAVITY MOVES SOUTH.
teach.b: Hold that next to an older picture of the church: stone cathedrals, pipe organs, northern winters.
Historians who study where Christians live now describe the church's center of gravity moving south, toward Africa, Latin America and parts of Asia.
They argue over the details and the figures, and this lesson leaves the figures to them. Some readers hear an echo of it in the book of Acts.
At Pentecost, Peter quotes the prophet Joel: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions". Daughters. Young men.
The Spirit does not wait for age or rank.

Paul writes to the Galatians: "there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." And in Acts the good news heads south almost at once.
An angel sends Philip "toward the south", down the desert road to Gaza. A chariot passes, carrying an official from Ethiopia who is reading Isaiah aloud.
Philip runs up beside it and asks, "Understandest thou what thou readest?" Before the chariot moves on, the man is baptized at the roadside water and goes on his way rejoicing.
To some readers, a young woman in Lagos or São Paulo as a face of the church sounds less like something new and more like those earliest chapters.
Churches differ on which roles women may hold: some ordain women as pastors and priests, some do not, and each side argues from scripture. This lesson ranks none of them.
It only notices who keeps showing up in choirs, kitchens and Sunday classes.

how: Christians across Africa, Latin America and Asia gather in large cathedrals and small rented rooms alike, where young women, among others, lead singing, teach children and visit the sick.

games.q: you're Philip, sent down a desert road heading south. a chariot rolls by: an official from Ethiopia, reading the prophet Isaiah aloud. what do you do?
o: keep walking; he's a stranger from far away.

games.why: Acts 8:30: Philip runs to him and asks, "understandest thou what thou readest?" before the road ends the official is baptized, and he goes on his way rejoicing.

practice: Hold one young woman of faith in mind: a niece, a coworker, the girl who reads at church, or someone you'll never meet, walking to a classroom church on another continent this Sunday.
Picture her morning, the iron, the walk, the songs. If you pray, you can pray for her strength and her joy; if you don't, just wish her well, steadily.

wordCard.voice: Lagos. A West African city whose young women, historians say, are one face of today's church, as Christianity's center of gravity moves south.

orig.note: Greek: church. in the New Testament it means a gathering of people, not a building.
